strengths: Addresses a meaningful limitation of causal and contextual Bayesian optimization: choosing which variables to intervene on and observe can change the attainable optimum. The introductory structural causal model provides a clear, analytically correct example.
Provides a simple framework combining causal policy-scope reduction with contextual optimization, extending existing mixed-policy ideas to continuous decision variables.

Experiments report 110 seeds, 700 interventions per run, and uncertainty intervals. They include settings where competing methods can attain the optimum and acknowledge a case where contextual BO converges faster.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited. Policy-scope characterization and pruning come from prior POMPS work, while optimization and scope selection use existing HEBO and standard UCB. This integration needs stronger theoretical or empirical evidence to establish a contribution competitive with top-tier submissions.

The UCB justification in Section 4.2 does not address its changing reward distributions: each arm represents an optimizer whose policy improves with additional evaluations. Stationarity at an assumed optimum does not establish that the allocation mechanism will reach that optimum. No analysis of the combined procedure is provided, and decreasing average regret over 700 iterations does not establish asymptotic sublinear regret or support the claim that the method always achieves the optimum.

Support for general mixed policy scopes is insufficiently specified. The definitions allow distinct information sets and contexts generated after upstream interventions, whereas the proposed acquisition rule jointly optimizes actions with a fixed context vector. The paper does not explain how this respects each intervention's permitted information or handles sequential decisions.

The experiments do not isolate the proposed scope selector. In both medical examples, CoCa-BO has only one POMPS, so UCB performs no selection; comparisons with CaBO therefore cannot establish that UCB causes the reported variance reduction. Comparisons against uniform allocation, alternative bandit selectors, and acquisition-based selection over identical candidate scopes are missing.

Evaluation is restricted to a few synthetic constructions, and every evaluated problem has only one or two POMPSes. The larger example mainly introduces redundant variables while retaining two candidate scopes. Without experiments varying the number of scopes, enumeration costs, or runtime, the claimed efficiency of scope search remains weakly supported.

Experimental specifications contain substantive inconsistencies. Appendix A.2 omits the Cancer term from the printed PSA equation but requires it for the completed-square derivation and claimed optimum. Appendix C defines C4 using itself, conflicting with the acyclic model. Section 5's regret sign also conflicts with the maximization experiments. These issues need reconciliation with the implementation; missing UCB settings, baseline configurations, and a code link further limit reproducibility.
